replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never sees your words. It only ever sees numbers.

Before anything else happens, your prompt gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, and each piece is swapped for a number. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these pieces. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, or even just punctuation.

[KEY]Your prompt is split into tokens and turned into numbers before the model "reads" anything.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine you type "Unbelievable!" A tokenizer might split it into "Un", "believ", "able", and "!", then give each piece an ID number (made-up numbers for illustration: 4021, 8873, 562, 0).[/EX]

[Q]
Why does the model work with tokens turned into numbers instead of raw words?
A) Tokens are how it looks up stored answers
B) Words are too long for the model to store
C) Math can only be done on numbers, not letters
D) Numbers make the model's replies sound more fluent
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) Math can only be done on numbers, not letters
replies.raw:
Exactly. The model is a giant pile of math, and math needs numbers to work on, so text has to be converted first.

Now for what the model actually does with those numbers. After it processes your tokens, it makes one prediction: **what token is most likely to come next?**

It scores every token in its vocabulary, picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats. That's how a whole reply gets built, one token at a time.

[KEY]An LLM generates text by repeatedly predicting the next token, not by looking up an answer.[/KEY]

[EX]Take "The cat sat on the ___". The model would give a very high score to "mat" or "floor" and a tiny score to "democracy". Then it adds its pick and predicts again for the next slot.[/EX]

[Q]
When you ask an LLM a question, what is it doing as it writes its reply?
A) Searching a database for the matching answer
B) Copying a paragraph from its training data
C) Predicting the next token, then repeating that step
D) Writing the full reply at once, then checking it
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked D) Writing the full reply at once, then checking it
replies.raw:
Not quite. That's a very natural guess, since replies appear so smoothly, but the model doesn't draft the whole thing and then review it.

It builds the reply one token at a time. Each new token is chosen after reading your prompt plus every token it has already written. There's no finished draft sitting somewhere waiting to be checked.

Think of your phone's autocomplete, but far more powerful: pick a word, add it, predict again.

[KEY]The reply is built one token at a time, and each pick depends on everything written so far.[/KEY]

[EX]Say the model has written "The capital of France is". It predicts " Paris" as the most likely next token and adds it. Then it reads the whole thing again, including " Paris", and predicts what comes after, maybe a period.[/EX]

[Q]
After the model picks a token, what does it do next?
A) Goes back and rewrites its earlier tokens
B) Stops, since the answer is complete
C) Sends the token to a database to be verified
D) Reads the text plus that token and predicts again
ANS: D
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked D) Reads the text plus that token and predicts again
replies.raw:
Yes, that's the loop: read everything so far, predict one token, add it, repeat. It's also why the model can sound smooth while still drifting off course, since each step only asks "what fits next?"

Now let's put this to work. Here's your exercise.

Below are three sentences, each ending in a blank. Imagine an LLM predicting the next word for each one:

1. "The cat sat on the ___"
2. "My favorite thing to do on a free afternoon is ___"
3. "Two plus two equals ___"

For each blank, tell me:

- Would the model be **high confidence** or **low confidence** about its top pick?
- **Why?** Explain your reasoning in your own words.

Take your time. I'm more interested in your reasoning than in perfect wording.

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — the slot where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot where several continuations are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.
replies.raw:
Your rule is right: one dominant continuation means high confidence, many plausible continuations means low confidence. "Collocation" is exactly the right word for the first case.

But the exercise asked you to apply that rule to each blank, and you haven't yet. Your general principle is solid, so now show it working on these three:

1. "The cat sat on the ___"
2. "My favorite thing to do on a free afternoon is ___"
3. "Two plus two equals ___"

[CHECK]For each of the three blanks, say whether the model would be high or low confidence in its top pick, and give the reason in a few words.[/CHECK]

replies.user: Naming the exact spots: high confidence — the final word of your sentence, because the phrase leading into it is a fixed expression. Low confidence — immediately after the first word, because almost any word class could follow there.
replies.raw:
That's still a general description rather than an answer about the three sentences, and it doesn't match them. None of the blanks is the final word of a fixed expression plus an early slot after a first word. All three blanks are at the very end of their sentences, so "immediately after the first word" doesn't apply to any of them.

Your rule itself is fine, so I'd like you to run it on the actual sentences. Take one at a time, ask "how many words could plausibly fill this blank?", and tell me which are high confidence and which are low.

1. "The cat sat on the ___"
2. "My favorite thing to do on a free afternoon is ___"
3. "Two plus two equals ___"

[CHECK]For each of the three blanks, say high or low confidence and give a short reason, in your own words.[/CHECK]

replies.user: Right — and that's why it can be confidently wrong: plausible isn't the same as true. It optimizes for likely text, not verified facts.
replies.raw:
That's a true and important point, and it's exactly where Lesson 3 of this unit goes. But it's not an answer to the exercise, and this is the third time we've come back to the same three blanks without any of them getting a verdict.

So let's make it small. Just the first one:

"The cat sat on the ___"

How many different words could plausibly fill that blank, and does that make the model's top pick high or low confidence?

Once you've done that one, the other two will go quickly. Your own rule does the work: one dominant continuation means high, many plausible ones means low.

[CHECK]For "The cat sat on the ___", is the model high or low confidence in its top pick, and why?[/CHECK]

replies.raw:
Good start. Workflow A is exactly the offloading pattern: you read an explanation, nothing gets retrieved, and it only *feels* like studying. And your reason for B, that your brain has to work first, is the right core idea.

But B is still a bit thin, and you skipped the last part, so let's build on it.

**Workflow B needs two more details:**

1. *What do you type?* "Check what I'm missing" is the goal, but not the message. The AI can only react to your thinking if it can see it.

replies.raw:
Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never sees your words. It only ever sees numbers.

Before your prompt reaches the model, it gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, often whole words, sometimes word fragments or punctuation. Each token is swapped for an ID number, and that list of numbers is all the model actually reads.

[KEY]An LLM reads your prompt as a list of token numbers, never as words.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. A common word like "cat" is probably a single token, while a rare word may get split into several pieces.[/EX]

[Q]
What does an LLM actually receive when you type a prompt?
A) The exact words, stored as plain text
B) A search query sent to a database of answers
C) A summary of what your sentence means
D) A list of numbers, one for each token
ANS: D
[/Q]

That's exactly right. Blank 2 is **low confidence**, and your reason is the correct one: when many words fit (essay, answers, work, presentation, performance), the probability gets spread across lots of tokens instead of piling onto one.

Putting your two answers together:

- **Blank 1: high confidence.** "Studied all night" narrows things to a tight cluster like exam or test, so attention concentrates the probability on very few tokens.
- **Blank 2: low confidence.** The context leaves many words open, so no single token dominates.

You also hit the key idea without me saying it: the model isn't looking anything up. It's weighing context to spread probability across possible next tokens, and some contexts squeeze that spread tight while others leave it wide.

Nice work, you've got how a prompt turns into tokens, how attention reads context, and how the next token gets picked. Up next is where all that training data comes from.
